card: In Amsterdam Hegel posted his letter, saw the second part of the picture gallery and the former town hall, which Napoleon had made an imperial palace and the royal family occupies when in the city. He visited a church noted for its coloured windows, lunched on fish with Dr. Besseling, a Catholic, and left by diligence at 5 pm.

After lunch Hegel went back to the post office in Kassel and booked a seat on the next day's diligence to Giessen, where the road to Koblenz leaves the Frankfurt road. While there he received a letter from his wife Marie.

Hegel and Mr. van Ghert spent four morning hours on foot in Antwerp. Its churches, like Ghent's, hold life-size marble statues; one church can contain two to three dozen large paintings by Rubens, van Dyck and their pupils. There the two parted: van Ghert returned to Brussels to ask after letters from Marie and send them to Amsterdam.

Hegel's plan to hire a coachman in Magdeburg with the Englishman fell through, so the two left by diligence at noon the day before, in a coach upholstered and lined with green morocco, and reached Brunswick about 5 am. There they saw the museum, chiefly its picture gallery, including the painting Government Plenipotentiary Schulz had mentioned to Hegel.

Hegel reached Magdeburg at 1 pm. The next coach to Kassel left on Tuesday noon. That afternoon he saw the cathedral, with cast apostles by Fischer of Nuremberg, called on General Carnot, and walked by the Elbe as 13 Hamburg ships sailed in. Next morning a coachman due to drive an Englishman to Kassel in three days arrived.

Hegel's diligence from Brunswick, carrying him and a 25- or 26-year-old Englishman bound from Italy for Paris, reached Northeim at 3 pm the previous day. As it would wait there until 8 or 9 pm, Hegel hired a post-chaise through Göttingen to Münden, arriving at 10 pm; after sleeping until 6 am he went on to Kassel.

Having come from Breda the day before via Moerdijk, a steamboat crossing of the Hollandsch Diep, Dordrecht, Rotterdam and Delft, Hegel went in the morning through the woods to Scheveningen, an hour away, and saw the North Sea. He then visited the picture gallery, walked in the Bois in the afternoon, and in the evening saw three French comedies.

Hegel arrived in Hamburg by ship about 10 am and had his luggage sent to the post office for that day's express coach, to be home by Monday. No seat was free, even for Wednesday; two letters from Marie were waiting. He was at the König von Hannover inn; the next possible departure was Monday's post wagon, arriving Thursday.

Hegel travelled via Abersau and Culm to Töplitz and lodged at a new inn with the sign of the King of Prussia. He then climbed the Schlackenberg opposite the inn, as Fräulein Stok had recommended, drank the waters in the Spitalgarten, walked in the park of Prince Clary's castle, bathed in the Steinbad and dined.

The weather was bad on Sunday afternoon. Having overlooked the unusual starting time on the playbill, Hegel reached the theatre only at 7 and missed the chorus 'Es lebe unser guter Kaiser Franz'. He then heard the first act of Zelmira, with Dardanelli, Donzelli and Lablache; Donzelli sang a recitative.
After the Prater, Hegel went to the Leopoldstadt theatre. A prelude was given in which Schuster played an elderly merchant with a young wife, followed once more by Die Zauberbirn.

Hegel revisited Prince Lichtenstein's gallery until 12 o'clock, then went to Währing, almost half an hour away, to look up Rembold, the local professor of philosophy. He crossed an arm of the Danube to lunch in the Augarten, walked through the Prater, and finished at the Leopoldstadt theatre, where Schuster played a Magister, followed by Die Zauberbirn.

Hegel arrived in Töplitz on Saturday afternoon and in Dresden the following evening. He went straight to Tiek's, where he found Professor Hinrichs, who was moving to Halle, and Friedrich von Schlegel, though Hegel learned who Schlegel was only after he had left.

From the Schloßberg Hegel viewed the Töplitz basin, 3 to 4 hours wide, between the mountains dividing Saxony from Bohemia and a second range to the south, with the Nollendorf church, Kulm, Marienschein and Aussig on the Elbe. He then walked around Töplitz and saw a few acts of Preciosa at the theatre.
Hegel stopped for the night at Duxan, which lies a little more than halfway along the road from Prague to Töplitz.
Hegel visited the greenhouses by the Burg, entering and leaving through a kind of underground passage which the Emperor uses every day when he spends some afternoon hours in his gardens.

Hegel and his party went to the English company at the Odeon, near where he lodged, rather than hear Pesaroni, who sang that evening. He had earlier seen Mlle Mars in Emilia, the only piece she was then appearing in.

Hegel was at table in Brussels with Mr. van Ghert, his wife and their six children, five boys and one girl; the eldest son was 17. The van Gherts sent their regards to Marie and let Hegel promise that they might come to Berlin in perhaps four years; the eldest son was to complete his studies in Berlin.

Hegel reached Weimar at sunset on 16 October and went to Goethe, where Riemer and Zelter were present. The Grand Duke came to tea half an hour later; Hegel sat beside him on the sofa and they conversed until 9:30. At 10 the next morning Hegel and Zelter drove in Goethe's carriage to the Grand Duke's botanical garden at Belvedere.

Hegel left by express post at 4 the previous morning and reached Trier, over 16 German miles away, at 8. On 28 August, from after 8 until 1:30, a brother of the innkeeper showed him the Roman ruins and the surrounding area, including an estate of the brother-in-law of Procurator-General Eichhorn. In the afternoon Hegel visited the churches.

Hegel moved out of the Hôtel des Princes in the morning and left his belongings for the time being at Cousin's; the two meant to find a furnished room (chambre garnie) that morning. At 11 they ate a short breakfast of cutlets with a bottle of wine, as Cousin was to get Hegel's letter to the post by 2.

Hegel arrived in Paris on Sunday between 10 and 11, took a room at the Hôtel des Princes and at once sought out Cousin. He saw from outside the Boulevards, Palais Royal, Louvre, Tuileries and Luxembourg. That evening he went to the Champs Élysées, with its carousel and cafés such as the Ambassadeurs and the Aurore, crowded with families.

Hegel boarded the diligence again at 3 p.m. the day before and reached Brussels at 6 a.m. He went to bed, had breakfast, received Marie's letter and wrote back at once, and was about to go out with his friend Cousin. He was to leave for Cologne the next morning, where he expected a letter from her.

After Hegel returned from an excursion, Cousin handed him a letter from Marie in which she wrote about his illness and her worries over it; his son Immanuel had also written, asking what had made him ill.
